title: At coroner's inquest, family of man shot dead by police pushes for change
subtitle: The family of a Southwestern Ontario man fatally shot by police after he charged at officers with an axe say they're participating in a coroner's inquest to save another family from the pain and trauma they've experienced.
article: The family of a Southwestern Ontario man fatally shot by police after he charged at officers with an axe say they're participating in a coroner's inquest to save another family from the pain and trauma they've experienced.

The inquest opened Monday into the death of Wade Vander Wal, 44, who was shot dead by two OPP officers outside his family's Exeter house on Dec. 3, 2019, after emergency crews were called to a fire at the home.
Vander Wal's mother and sister spoke Monday at the opening of the inquest expected to last 10 days and hear from 11 witnesses.
The family members, neither of whom will testify at the inquest, described the lasting psychological toll of Vander Wal's violent death, and the media coverage of it.

"We struggle to find the value of placing our time, energy, finances and emotions into a process that so many have found less than effective," Vander Wal's sister Sandy said of taking part in the inquest process.
An inquest is a formal hearing during which the facts of the death are laid out before a jury, who may make non-binding recommendations to prevent similar deaths from occurring.
But enduring the pain the inquest will bring up may prevent future deaths, the family concluded.

"It will be worth it if there's a chance that changes can be made that will prevent even one other person from losing their life in a mental health crisis or one other family having to go through this process," Sandy said. "So, we ask you the jury, what can you recommend (that will prevent) from this happening again and again? How do we ensure that this is just not words and wishes?"
Inquest counsel Jar Dhar provided an overview of the anticipated evidence witnesses are expected to deliver, adding there may be "conflicting versions of some of the details."

Exeter resident Patricia Baker got a call from her teenage son around 6 p.m., saying Vander Wal had come to the house and was acting strangely. She came home and went to Vander Wal's home, where he was speaking about the military and acting erratically.
Diane Vander Wal came home and her son, who has bipolar disorder, became increasingly irritated, so she went to Baker's home and the two women decided Baker would try to talk to Vander Wal again.

While speaking to Vander Wal, Baker noticed what appeared to be a small fire in the kitchen - it was later determined to be a smoldering bag of cigarettes - and urged him to leave the house, but he refused.
Baker returned home to call 911 and told dispatchers her neighbour was experiencing a mental health episode and was inside his home with a fire burning.
Firefighters arrived first and tried to convince Vander Wal to leave, but he refused. An OPP officer showed up and also was unsuccessful at convincing Vander Wal to exit the house.

Two more OPP officers arrived and a battering ram was used to knock down the door. Vander Wal emerged with an axe in his hand and advanced toward officers, one of whom deployed their conducted-energy weapon (CEW).

"But the CEV had no effect and Wade continued to advance toward the officers with the axe. At this point Wade was in front of the house as the officers backed away. Officers then discharged firearms several times and Wade went to the ground," Dhar said.
Wade still had the axe on the ground and an officer used their conducted-energy weapon, while another officer tried to get the axe away from Vander Wal.

"Now, there may be conflicting evidence (about) what happened next, but I anticipate that at least some witnesses will testify that they thought that (the officer) was infected by the energy from the CEW when he went to get the axe from Wade," Dhar said. "And it appeared, I believe some witnesses will say . . . that some sort of struggle ensured between (the officer) and Vander Wal."
Another officer fired shots again and Vander Wal fell to the ground. He was taken to the hospital and pronounced dead.
Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), cleared the officers involved of any wrongdoing.
Emergency dispatches were played for the jury Monday before the inquest heard from South Huron fire Chief Jeffrey Musser, the first emergency responder to arrive on the scene.
Musser spoke with Vander Wal, who remained inside the house. Musser said he couldn't see any smoke.
Police arrived and used a battering ram to open the door before Vander Wal emerged with a hatchet in his right hand, Musser said.

"I believe he meant to harm someone," Musser said. "The way he came out of the door, he wasn't taking his time. He was charging . . . (his) body language tells me, 'That person was out to hurt someone.'"
The inquest continues Tuesday.
